claims.text: Adding a strongly coordinating ligand during solution-phase synthesis promotes uniform atomic mixing in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
The ligand promotes uniform atomic mixing by stabilizing early nucleation sites.
More uniform atomic mixing leads to reliable formation of a single-phase HEA structure.
Reliable formation of a single-phase HEA structure enhances catalytic performance relative to nanoparticles synthesized without the ligand.
PVP is an example of a strongly coordinating ligand suitable for this intervention.
The ligand-assisted and no-ligand syntheses will be compared at the same temperature, precursor concentration, and reducing conditions.
The proposed structural mediator is a uniform atomic distribution with suppressed phase segregation.
The ligand binds to multiple metal centers during nucleation.
Binding of the ligand to multiple metal centers lowers the kinetic barrier for co-nucleation.
A lower co-nucleation barrier homogenizes the metal distribution in the nanoparticles.
A homogenized metal distribution produces fewer compositional fluctuations.
Fewer compositional fluctuations provide more uniform catalytically active surface sites.
Ligand-assisted synthesis will yield a more uniform elemental distribution than otherwise identical synthesis without the ligand.
Ligand-assisted nanoparticles will exhibit improved catalytic activity, represented by higher turnover frequency or lower onset potential.
The hypothesis applies to noble metal–based HEA catalysts prepared by solution-phase reduction, especially when catalysis is sensitive to active-surface homogeneity.
Hydrogen evolution is an example of a reaction whose performance may be sensitive to active-surface homogeneity.
TEM/EDS mapping can be used to compare atomic-distribution homogeneity between the ligand-assisted and control samples.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in either atomic homogeneity or catalytic performance in the ligand-assisted sample would falsify the hypothesis.
